title: Adaptive repairlets: contextual, safety-gated admin utilities
creator: Marisol Ortega
description:
Goal: Convert a subset of high-frequency, low-complexity runbook steps into small, idempotent 'repairlets' that can be executed interactively by oncall and optionally by the autopilot runner. Repairlets are purpose-built admin utilities: single-responsibility units (e.g., rotate-failed-node, clear-eviction-cache, refresh-kv-prefix) that carry embedded safety checks, telemetry assertions, and an approved rollback path.

Why now: We have recurring incidents where engineers repeatedly perform the same sequence of guarded steps to remediate transient inference-worker failures (KV cache corruption, stuck batches, GPU memory pressure). These steps are well-understood but error-prone when done manually under stress. Repairlets reduce human error, standardize audit trails, and enable safe partial automation.

Key design principles:
- Single responsibility: each repairlet does one thing and has a clear precondition/postcondition.
- Idempotency: running a repairlet multiple times should leave the system in the same state or be safely no-op.
- Telemetry gating: each repairlet checks SLO and signal conditions (error rate, queue-depth, KV-miss-rate) before running; abort with a clear reason if preconditions fail.
- Safety modes: interactive (operator confirms), constrained autopilot (requires multi-signal and rate limits), and dry-run (no changes, only simulated outcomes).
- Audit & provenance: every execution writes an immutable audit event with inputs, operator id, feature-flag version, and correlated trace id.
- Rollback recipe: a concise, tested rollback step is bundled with each repairlet.

Scope for this ticket: prototype three repairlets and the minimal orchestration around them (registry, execution API, audit sink):
1) repairlet/eviction-recover: gracefully drain and restart a stuck eviction-worker process, with KV prefetch validation.
2) repairlet/kv-prefix-refresh: refresh prefix cache for a tenant, with telemetry checks to ensure cache fill-rate improves.
3) repairlet/gpu-memory-defrag: trigger a controlled service restart of offending container and optionally adjust oom_score_adj for that job.

Out-of-scope: full autopilot rollout; internal UI improvements beyond basic execution page; RBAC integration beyond a single ops group.
acceptance_criteria: Three repairlets implemented in the repairlet registry with documented preconditions and rollback recipes.
Each repairlet exposes: dry-run, interactive-exec (requires operator confirmation), and constrained-autopilot flags.
Automated unit tests covering idempotency and telemetry gating for each repairlet.
Execution events emitted to audit-log (s3) and shown in the operator execution dashboard with trace links.
A canary execution runbook demonstrating operator flow and one simulated autopilot run in staging without side effects.
implementation_notes:
High-level plan:
1) Repairlet runtime: small Go binary library (existing ops-toolkit language) that receives: repairlet-id, inputs, mode, operator-id, trace-context. It will call into existing admin RPCs. Use existing admin-client v2.
2) Registry: declarative YAML entries in repo/services/repairlets/ describing metadata (id, owner, preconditions, inputs, rollback, schema). Registry is loaded by the execution service at startup.
3) Execution API: /admin/repairlets/execute (POST) on the operator controlplane. Interactive flow will require a preflight POST -> token -> confirm POST to separate endpoint to reduce accidental double-exec.
4) Telemetry gating: build small gating lib that evaluates rules against Prometheus and trace logs (examples: last-10m error_rate>0.5% AND kv_miss_rate>3%). Rules are declarative in the YAML.
5) Audit: emit structured events to existing audit-log pipeline (kafka->s3) with the schema used by oncall playbooks. Include a link to the console trace and the Git SHA of the repairlet registry.
6) Safety knobs: feature-flag per-repairlet (FF) and global rate limiter using token-bucket stored in redis.
7) Testing: unit tests + staging integration harness that can run dry-run and simulated state changes. We'll add a chaos test that flips the gating metrics to ensure gating aborts.

Trade-offs / open questions:
- Where to author repairlet YAMLs long-term? Confluence vs git-as-source-of-truth — we prefer git for CI and PR review, but authoring UX is poorer.
- Execution language: Go keeps runtime compatibility; Python would be faster to iterate. Chosen: Go for now due to existing ops-toolkit ecosystem.
- Telemetry signal ownership: some signals are owned by the runtime team (KV miss); need product approval to use them in gating rules.

Follow-ups: RBAC expansion (owners, escalation groups), UI for constructing inputs, autopilot policy to safely run repairlets under specific conditions.
